claim: ASK1 dysregulation has been associated with cancer and inflammatory, cardiovascular, and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: ASK1 dysregulation has been associated with cancer and inflammatory, cardiovascular, and neurodegenerative diseases, among others.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific literature in the field.

claim: ASK1 is a multidomain Ser/Thr protein kinase regulated by a complex mechanism involving dimerization and interactions with several other proteins, including thioredoxin 1 (TRX1).
source: Nevertheless, as a multidomain Ser/Thr protein kinase, ASK1 is regulated by a complex mechanism involving dimerization and interactions with several other proteins, including thioredoxin 1 (TRX1).
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: In a state close to its active form, ASK1 is a compact and asymmetric dimer.
source: As shown by cryo-EM analysis, in a state close to its active form, ASK1 is a compact and asymmetric dimer, which enables extensive interdomain and interchain interactions.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by cryo-EM structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The compact and asymmetric ASK1 dimer enables extensive interdomain and interchain interactions.
source: As shown by cryo-EM analysis, in a state close to its active form, ASK1 is a compact and asymmetric dimer, which enables extensive interdomain and interchain interactions.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structural analysis showing the dimer architecture.

claim: Interdomain and interchain interactions in ASK1 stabilize the active conformation of the ASK1 kinase domain.
source: These interactions stabilize the active conformation of the ASK1 kinase domain.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from cryo-EM showing the kinase domain conformation.

claim: TRX1 functions as a negative allosteric effector of ASK1.
source: In turn, TRX1 functions as a negative allosteric effector of ASK1, modifying the structure of the TRX1-binding domain and changing its interaction with the tetratricopeptide repeats domain.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data showing structural changes upon TRX1 binding.

claim: TRX1 modifies the structure of the TRX1-binding domain and changes its interaction with the tetratricopeptide repeats domain.
source: In turn, TRX1 functions as a negative allosteric effector of ASK1, modifying the structure of the TRX1-binding domain and changing its interaction with the tetratricopeptide repeats domain.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data showing changes in deuteration patterns upon TRX1 binding.

claim: TRX1 reduces access to the activation segment of the kinase domain.
source: Consequently, TRX1 reduces access to the activation segment of the kinase domain.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data showing reduced deuteration in the activation segment upon TRX1 binding.

claim: MAP kinase cascades are one of the most important signal transduction networks in cells.
source: Mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase cascades are one of the most important signal transduction networks in cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell signaling.

claim: MAP kinase pathways are highly conserved throughout eukaryotes.
source: Highly conserved throughout eukaryotes (Widmann et al., 1999), MAP kinase pathways are activated in response to a number of stimuli, such as cytokines, growth factors, oxidative stress, calcium influx, and lipopolysaccharides, promoting proliferation, inflammatory responses, and apoptosis (Cuevas et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Widmann et al., 1999.

claim: MAP kinase pathways are activated in response to cytokines, growth factors, oxidative stress, calcium influx, and lipopolysaccharides.
source: Highly conserved throughout eukaryotes (Widmann et al., 1999), MAP kinase pathways are activated in response to a number of stimuli, such as cytokines, growth factors, oxidative stress, calcium influx, and lipopolysaccharides, promoting proliferation, inflammatory responses, and apoptosis (Cuevas et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cuevas et al., 2007.

claim: MAP kinase pathways promote proliferation, inflammatory responses, and apoptosis.
source: Highly conserved throughout eukaryotes (Widmann et al., 1999), MAP kinase pathways are activated in response to a number of stimuli, such as cytokines, growth factors, oxidative stress, calcium influx, and lipopolysaccharides, promoting proliferation, inflammatory responses, and apoptosis (Cuevas et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cuevas et al., 2007.

claim: The MAP kinase system is composed of three layers: MAP3K, MAP2K, and MAPK.
source: The incoming signals are transmitted across a common, three-layered protein kinase system composed of the upstream MAP kinase kinase kinase (MAP3K), the intermediate MAP kinase kinase (MAP2K), and the downstream MAP kinase (MAPK) (Widmann et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Widmann et al., 1999.

claim: MAP2Ks and MAPKs are activated through phosphorylation by an upstream kinase.
source: MAP2Ks and MAPKs are similarly activated through phosphorylation by an upstream kinase, but MAP3K activation is much more complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge in MAP kinase signaling.

claim: MAP3K activation is much more complex than MAP2K and MAPK activation.
source: MAP2Ks and MAPKs are similarly activated through phosphorylation by an upstream kinase, but MAP3K activation is much more complex.
evidence: This is supported by the context of the manuscript and general knowledge.

claim: MAP3Ks require tight regulation given the high number of their potential triggers and the serious consequences of their dysregulation.
source: MAP3Ks require a tight regulation given the high number of their potential triggers and the serious consequences of their dysregulation, in the form of various diseases (Fujino et al., 2007; Peti and Page, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fujino et al., 2007 and Peti and Page, 2013.

claim: Cancer and inflammatory, cardiovascular, and neurodegenerative diseases have been extensively associated with excessive ASK1 signaling.
source: Cancer and inflammatory, cardiovascular, and neurodegenerative diseases, among others, have been extensively associated with excessive ASK1 signaling, in particular (Katome et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2019; Meijles et al., 2020; Okazaki, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ASK1 directs cells toward apoptosis, differentiation, and senescence via the p38 and JNK MAP kinase pathways.
source: Also known as MAP3K5, ASK1 stands out for its role in directing cells toward apoptosis, differentiation, and senescence via the p38 and JNK MAP kinase pathways (Ichijo et al., 1997; Sawada et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ichijo et al., 1997 and Sawada et al., 2001.

claim: Currently available JNK and p38 inhibitors lack efficacy and/or have undesirable side effects.
source: However, currently available JNK and p38 inhibitors lack efficacy and/or have undesirable side effects (Bühler and Laufer, 2014; Ijaz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bühler and Laufer, 2014 and Ijaz et al., 2009.

claim: ASK1 is a prospective target for therapeutic intervention in diseases associated with excessive ASK1 signaling.
source: Therefore, as their upstream activator, ASK1 is a prospective target for therapeutic intervention in these disorders, especially considering its wide range of triggers and interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of current inhibitors and ASK1's role in disease.

claim: Various stress stimuli, such as oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and calcium influx, activate ASK1.
source: Various stress stimuli, such as oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and calcium influx, activate ASK1, thus explaining why this Ser/Thr-specific protein kinase is such a crucial stress sensor (Ichijo et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ichijo et al., 1997.

claim: Human ASK1 is a multi-domain protein consisting of TBD, CRR (formed by TPR and PH domains), KD, and a C-terminal CC region followed by a SAM domain.
source: In line with this function, human ASK1 is a multi-domain protein consisting of an N-terminal thioredoxin-binding domain (TBD), a central regulatory region (CRR) formed by tetratricopeptide repeats (TPR), and pleckstrin-homology (PH) domains, a kinase domain (KD), and a C-terminal coiled-coil (CC) region followed by a sterile alpha motif (SAM) domain (Figure 1A; Bunkoczi et al., 2007; Psenakova et al., 2020; Trevelyan et al., 2020; Weijman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1A showing the domain structure.

claim: In both resting and active states, ASK1 forms a large multiprotein complex, the ASK signalosome, with dozens of interacting proteins.
source: In both resting and active states, ASK1 forms a large multiprotein complex, the ASK signalosome, with dozens of interacting proteins, including other ASK family members ASK2 and ASK3 (Federspiel et al., 2016; Kaji et al., 2010; Saitoh et al., 1998; Subramanian et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the resting state, ASK1 constitutively oligomerizes, presumably via the C-terminal CC region and the SAM domain.
source: In the resting state, ASK1 constitutively oligomerizes, presumably via the C-terminal CC region and the SAM domain, remaining inactive through interactions with TRX1, glutaredoxin and 14-3-3 proteins (Bunkoczi et al., 2007; Fujino et al., 2007; Kosek et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2000; Petrvalska et al., 2016; Psenakova et al., 2020; Saitoh et al., 1998; Subramanian et al., 2004; Tobiume et al., 2002; Trevelyan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ASK1 remains inactive through interactions with TRX1, glutaredoxin and 14-3-3 proteins.
source: In the resting state, ASK1 constitutively oligomerizes, presumably via the C-terminal CC region and the SAM domain, remaining inactive through interactions with TRX1, glutaredoxin and 14-3-3 proteins (Bunkoczi et al., 2007; Fujino et al., 2007; Kosek et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2000; Petrvalska et al., 2016; Psenakova et al., 2020; Saitoh et al., 1998; Subramanian et al., 2004; Tobiume et al., 2002; Trevelyan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: TRX1 binding to the N-terminal TBD is thought to prevent homophilic interactions between ASK1 N-termini.
source: Although the exact role of these binding partners in ASK1 regulation is still debated, TRX1 binding to the N-terminal TBD is thought to prevent homophilic interactions between ASK1 N-termini containing the TBD, TPR, PH, and KD domains (Fujino et al., 2007; Weijman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fujino et al., 2007 and Weijman et al., 2017.

claim: When complexed with TRX1, inactive ASK1 is ubiquitinated and degraded.
source: When complexed with TRX1, inactive ASK1 is ubiquitinated and degraded (Liu and Min, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu and Min, 2002.

claim: Under oxidative stress, TRX1 oxidation triggers its dissociation from the ASK signalosome.
source: By contrast, under oxidative stress, TRX1 oxidation triggers its dissociation from the ASK signalosome, followed by 14-3-3 dissociation and tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor (TRAF2/5/6) recruitment to CRR (Fujino et al., 2007; Goldman et al., 2004; Gotoh and Cooper, 1998; Kylarova et al., 2016; Nadeau et al., 2009; Nadeau et al., 2007; Saitoh et al., 1998; Noguchi et al., 2005; Psenakova et al., 2020; Song and Lee, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: TRX1 dissociation is followed by 14-3-3 dissociation and TRAF2/5/6 recruitment to CRR.
source: By contrast, under oxidative stress, TRX1 oxidation triggers its dissociation from the ASK signalosome, followed by 14-3-3 dissociation and tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor (TRAF2/5/6) recruitment to CRR (Fujino et al., 2007; Goldman et al., 2004; Gotoh and Cooper, 1998; Kylarova et al., 2016; Nadeau et al., 2009; Nadeau et al., 2007; Saitoh et al., 1998; Noguchi et al., 2005; Psenakova et al., 2020; Song and Lee, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Daxx directly interacts with ASK1, presumably through CRR or another ASK1 domain N-terminal to KD.
source: Presumably through CRR or another ASK1 domain N-terminal to KD, death domain-associated protein 6 (Daxx) directly interacts with ASK1, thereby mediating ASK1 activation by the death-inducing ligand system, known as cluster of differentiation 95 (CD95)/Fas receptor (Chang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chang et al., 1998.

claim: Daxx mediates ASK1 activation by the CD95/Fas receptor.
source: Presumably through CRR or another ASK1 domain N-terminal to KD, death domain-associated protein 6 (Daxx) directly interacts with ASK1, thereby mediating ASK1 activation by the death-inducing ligand system, known as cluster of differentiation 95 (CD95)/Fas receptor (Chang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chang et al., 1998.

claim: Homophilic interactions between ASK1 N-termini lead to Thr838 phosphorylation in the activation segment.
source: These events likely enable homophilic interactions between ASK1 N-termini, leading to Thr838 phosphorylation in the activation segment either by trans-autophosphorylation or by protein serine/threonine kinase 38 (MPK38) and subsequent ASK1 activation (Jung et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2000; Nadeau et al., 2007; Tobiume et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Thr838 phosphorylation occurs either by trans-autophosphorylation or by MPK38.
source: These events likely enable homophilic interactions between ASK1 N-termini, leading to Thr838 phosphorylation in the activation segment either by trans-autophosphorylation or by protein serine/threonine kinase 38 (MPK38) and subsequent ASK1 activation (Jung et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2000; Nadeau et al., 2007; Tobiume et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: C-terminally truncated ASK1 forms a compact and asymmetric dimer with all four N-terminal domains involved in extensive interdomain and interchain interactions.
source: The cryo-EM map revealed that C-terminally truncated ASK1 forms a compact and asymmetric dimer, enabling extensive interdomain and interchain interactions (Figure 1B and C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figures 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: One side of the ASK1 molecule is formed by TBD and TPR domains of both protomers, with TBD domains embedded between TPR domains.
source: One side of the molecule is formed by TBD and TPR domains of both protomers, with TBD domains embedded between TPR domains.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The TPR domains interact with a dimer of PH domains, and the resulting dimeric TBD-TPR-PH module has a funnel shape with approximately twofold rotational symmetry.
source: The TPR domains then interact with a dimer of PH domains, and the resulting dimeric TBD-TPR-PH module has a funnel shape with approximately twofold rotational symmetry.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The other side of the ASK1 molecule is formed by a KD dimer, which interacts with the N-terminal TBD-TPR-PH module through the KD of only one protomer.
source: The other side of the molecule is formed by a KD dimer, which interacts with the N-terminal TBD-TPR-PH module through the KD of only one protomer.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The binding site of one KD is located at the interface between the TPR and PH domains of the opposite protomer.
source: The binding site of this KD is located at the interface between the TPR and PH domains of the opposite protomer, and the second KD has no contact with the N-terminal domains of either its own or the other chain.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The second KD has no contact with the N-terminal domains of either its own or the other chain.
source: The binding site of this KD is located at the interface between the TPR and PH domains of the opposite protomer, and the second KD has no contact with the N-terminal domains of either its own or the other chain.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: TBD consists of a six-stranded, mostly parallel, β-sheet decorated with several α-helices, resembling the thioredoxin structure.
source: This model suggested that TBD consists of a six-stranded, mostly parallel, β-sheet decorated with several α-helices, thus resembling the thioredoxin structure.
evidence: This is supported by the AlphaFold model and cryo-EM map.

claim: TBD is a compact and globular domain that interacts with the TPR domain of the opposite protomer via the helix α3 and the loop between α4 and β5.
source: TBD is a compact and globular domain that interacts with the TPR domain of the opposite protomer via the helix α3 and the loop between α4 and β5.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The C-terminal helix α5 of TBD is connected by a short loop to helix α6, which is the first helix of the TPR domain.
source: The C-terminal helix α5 of TBD is connected by a short loop to helix α6, which is the first helix of the TPR domain.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In the same chain, there are no other contacts between TBD and TPR except for the interaction between the C-terminus of helix α3 of TBD and the N-terminus of helix α6 of TPR.
source: In the same chain, there are no other contacts between TBD and TPR except for the interaction between the C-terminus of helix α3 of TBD and the N-terminus of helix α6 of TPR.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Cysteine C250 is a crucial residue for TBD structural integrity and TRX1 binding.
source: In a previous study, cysteine C250, located at the N-terminus of α5, was identified as a crucial residue for TBD structural integrity and TRX1 binding (Kosek et al., 2014; Psenakova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: C250 forms a disulfide bridge with cysteine C225 located nearby.
source: Corroborating these findings, our structure of TBDA suggests that this cysteine residue forms a disulfide bridge with cysteine C225 located nearby (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The disulfide bridge between C225 and C250 was shown previously.
source: This disulfide, whose formation was shown previously (Kylarova et al., 2016), likely stabilizes the region containing residues 216–245 located between β5 and α5.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kylarova et al., 2016.

claim: The disulfide bridge between C225 and C250 likely stabilizes the region containing residues 216–245 located between β5 and α5.
source: This disulfide, whose formation was shown previously (Kylarova et al., 2016), likely stabilizes the region containing residues 216–245 located between β5 and α5.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: No interpretable density was found for residues 228–245 in both TBDs.
source: In addition, this region appears to be very flexible as no interpretable density was found for residues 228–245 in both TBDs.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The region containing residues 228–245 is very flexible.
source: In addition, this region appears to be very flexible as no interpretable density was found for residues 228–245 in both TBDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of interpretable density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: Isolated TBD retains substantial conformational plasticity.
source: This result is consistent with a previous NMR characterization of isolated TBD, which showed that this domain retains substantial conformational plasticity (Psenakova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Psenakova et al., 2020.

claim: The conformation of both CRR domains resembles the crystal structure of isolated CRR, with 14 tightly arranged α-helices forming seven tetratricopeptide repeats, followed by a PH domain.
source: The conformation of both CRR domains resembles the crystal structure of isolated CRR, with 14 tightly arranged α-helices (α6-α19) forming seven tetratricopeptide repeats (TPRs), followed by a PH domain (Weijman et al., 2017; Figure 1C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Superpositions with the crystal structure showed minor helix shifts in the first four repeats of both TPRs, most likely due to interactions with the TBD of the opposite chain.
source: Superpositions with the crystal structure showed minor helix shifts in the first four repeats of both TPRs, most likely due to interactions with the TBD of the opposite chain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both CRRs interact directly only through the β-sheets of their PH domains.
source: Both CRRs interact directly only through the β-sheets of their PH domains, and the resulting CRR dimer has twofold rotational symmetry (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: The resulting CRR dimer has twofold rotational symmetry.
source: Both CRRs interact directly only through the β-sheets of their PH domains, and the resulting CRR dimer has twofold rotational symmetry (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Extensive interactions between N-terminal TBD, TPR, and PH domains are a crucial factor for the homodimerization of C-terminally truncated ASK1.
source: Combined, extensive interactions between N-terminal TBD, TPR, and PH domains emerge as a crucial factor for the homodimerization of C-terminally truncated ASK1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: TPR and PH domains of one chain create a docking platform for the KD of the opposite chain.
source: TPR and PH domains of one chain (chain A) create a docking platform for the KD of the opposite chain (KDB), which interacts with TPRs 4 (helices α12, α13) and 7 (helices α18, α19) of TPRA, and β6 and β7 strands of PHA, mainly via its C-lobe (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: KDB interacts with TPRs 4 and 7 of TPRA, and β6 and β7 strands of PHA, mainly via its C-lobe.
source: TPR and PH domains of one chain (chain A) create a docking platform for the KD of the opposite chain (KDB), which interacts with TPRs 4 (helices α12, α13) and 7 (helices α18, α19) of TPRA, and β6 and β7 strands of PHA, mainly via its C-lobe (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The kinase domains of both protomers dimerize in a head-to-tail orientation through an extensive interface spanning almost the entire length of the domain.
source: The kinase domains of both protomers dimerize, as previously observed in the crystal structure of isolated ASK1 KD with bound inhibitor staurosporine (Bunkoczi et al., 2007), i.e., in a head-to-tail orientation through an extensive interface spanning almost the entire length of the domain.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with the crystal structure cited.

claim: Comparison with the crystal structure showed changes in the position of the αC helix, which is in the inward active position, in both KDs.
source: However, its comparison with the crystal structure showed changes in the position of the αC (α21) helix, which is in the inward active position, in both KDs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: The shift in the αC helix positions the conserved active site lysine (K709) within hydrogen-bond distance of the αC glutamate (E725).
source: This shift positions the conserved active site lysine (K709) within the hydrogen-bond distance of the αC glutamate (E725), as usually found in active kinases (Johnson et al., 1996; Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and citation to Johnson et al., 1996.

claim: The cryo-EM map of KDB enabled building the whole activation segment (residues 822–849).
source: The cryo-EM map of KDB, which interacts with TPRA and PHA domains, enabled us to build the whole activation segment (residues 822–849).
evidence: This is directly supported by the cryo-EM data.

claim: The activation segment of KDB adopts a conformation competent for substrate binding.
source: This segment adopts a conformation competent for substrate binding (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A similar conformation of the activation segment was observed in the crystal structure of ASK1 KD.
source: A similar conformation was observed in the crystal structure of ASK1 KD, which, however, showed only the beginning and end of the activation segment (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B; Bunkoczi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with the crystal structure.

claim: In the active conformation, the conserved residue E725 from the αC helix is within hydrogen-bond distance of the main chain of the DFG motif residues F823 and G824.
source: In this conformation, the conserved residue E725 from the αC (α21) helix is within the hydrogen-bond distance of the main chain of the DFG motif residues F823 and G824 at the beginning of the activation segment (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3E.

claim: A similar conformation of the activation segment was observed in the active form of BRAF.
source: A similar conformation of the activation segment was also observed in the active form of another MAP3K BRAF (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C; Haling et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with the BRAF structure.

claim: In active BRAF, the conformation of the activation segment is stabilized by E611 interactions with R575 from the catalytic HRD motif.
source: In active BRAF, the conformation of the activation segment is stabilized by E611 interactions with R575 from the catalytic HRD motif, but in the KDB of the present structure, the activation segment is stabilized by interactions with the α18 and α19 helices from the last TPR repeat of the TPRA domain (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with the BRAF structure and the current cryo-EM structure.

claim: In KDB, the activation segment is stabilized by interactions with the α18 and α19 helices from the last TPR repeat of the TPRA domain.
source: In active BRAF, the conformation of the activation segment is stabilized by E611 interactions with R575 from the catalytic HRD motif, but in the KDB of the present structure, the activation segment is stabilized by interactions with the α18 and α19 helices from the last TPR repeat of the TPRA domain (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The activation segment of KDA is not visible in the cryo-EM map, likely due to its high flexibility.
source: The activation segment of the KD domain from the opposite chain (KDA), which has no contact with N-terminal domains, is not visible in our map, likely due to its high flexibility.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The beginning and end of the activation segment of KDA adopt a conformation similar to that observed in the crystal structure of the isolated ASK1 KD.
source: However, the beginning and end of this segment adopt a conformation similar to that observed in the crystal structure of the isolated ASK1 KD (Bunkoczi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with the crystal structure.

claim: The inward position of the helix αC and the conformation of the activation segment suggest that KDA is also in an active conformation.
source: Together with the inward position of the helix αC (α21), this conformation suggests that KDA is also in an active conformation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural features shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Comparison with the crystal structure of isolated KD revealed a change in the relative position of the KD subunits.
source: The comparison with the crystal structure of isolated KD revealed a change in the relative position of the KD subunits.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: KDB is slightly rotated relative to the equatorial plane of the dimer due to interactions of its C-lobe with TPRA.
source: KDB is slightly rotated relative to the equatorial plane of the dimer due to interactions of its C-lobe with TPRA.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The rotation of KDB results in a ~4 Å shift of the C-lobe relative to its position in the crystal structure of the KD dimer.
source: This rotation results in a~4 Å shift of the C-lobe relative to its position in the crystal structure of the KD dimer.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: Interdomain interactions within ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD stabilize the conformation of the activation segment.
source: Overall, interdomain interactions within ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD stabilize the conformation of the activation segment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The activation segment remains competent for substrate binding.
source: As a result, the activation segment remains competent for substrate binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural conformation.

claim: Isolated KD forms a stable dimer with a KD of ~220 nM.
source: Previous studies have shown that isolated KD forms a stable dimer with a KD of ~220 nM in which the protomers are oriented in a head-to-tail manner and interact through a large dimerization interface (Bunkoczi et al., 2007; Petrvalska et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The sedimentation coefficient distribution of isolated ASK1 KD showed only one peak with sw(20,w) of 4.2 S, corresponding to the KD dimer.
source: The sedimentation coefficient distribution c(s) of the isolated ASK1 KD assessed by SV AUC showed only one peak with weight-average sedimentation coefficients corrected to 20.0 °C and to the density of water, sw(20,w), of 4.2 S (estimated Mw~62 kDa), most likely corresponding to the KD dimer (the theoretical Mw of the KD dimer is 72.4 kDa) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by SV AUC data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Isolated TBD and CRR were protomeric in solution.
source: In contrast, the isolated domains, TBD and CRR, were protomeric in solution as their sedimentation coefficient distributions c(s) showed peaks with sw(20,w) of 2.2 and 3.3 S with estimated Mw∼16 kDa and ∼38 kDa, respectively (theoretical Mw of TBD and CRR are 20.6 and 45.5 kDa, respectively) (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by SV AUC data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: ASK1 TBD-CRR showed concentration-dependent dimerization.
source: While the ASK1 TBD-CRR construct showed concentration-dependent dimerization, as indicated by its bimodal c(s) distribution (Figure 3D), the ASK1 CRR-KD construct formed a stable dimer in solution, with a sw(20,w) of 6.9 S (estimated Mw∼166 kDa, theoretical Mw 163 kDa) (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by SV AUC data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ASK1 CRR-KD formed a stable dimer in solution, with a sw(20,w) of 6.9 S.
source: While the ASK1 TBD-CRR construct showed concentration-dependent dimerization, as indicated by its bimodal c(s) distribution (Figure 3D), the ASK1 CRR-KD construct formed a stable dimer in solution, with a sw(20,w) of 6.9 S (estimated Mw∼166 kDa, theoretical Mw 163 kDa) (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by SV AUC data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD formed stable dimers in solution, with a sw(20,w) of 8.5 S.
source: Similarly, as shown by its c(s) distribution, the longest ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD construct also formed stable dimers in solution, with a sw(20,w) of 8.5 S (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by SV AUC data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The sedimentation coefficient of 8.5 S for ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD is consistent with the theoretical sedimentation coefficient value of 9 S calculated using the HydroPRO program and the cryo-EM structure.
source: This value is consistent with the theoretical sedimentation coefficient value of 9 S calculated using the HydroPRO program (Ortega et al., 2011) and the cryo-EM structure of the ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD dimer.
evidence: This is supported by computational calculation and comparison with experimental data.

claim: The c(s) distribution of ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD revealed higher oligomers, whose abundance increased with concentration.
source: The c(s) distribution of ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD also revealed higher oligomers, whose abundance increased with the concentration.
evidence: This is supported by SV AUC data.

claim: The dimerization of KD-containing ASK1 constructs is not surprising because KDs form stable dimers, and CRRs do not interfere with the dimerization interface.
source: The dimerization of KD-containing ASK1 constructs is not surprising because KDs form stable dimers, and CRRs do not interfere with the dimerization interface; on the contrary, they facilitate dimerization through interactions between PH domains (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: CRRs facilitate dimerization through interactions between PH domains.
source: The dimerization of KD-containing ASK1 constructs is not surprising because KDs form stable dimers, and CRRs do not interfere with the dimerization interface; on the contrary, they facilitate dimerization through interactions between PH domains (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: The absence of dimerization of isolated TBD is consistent with its interactions within the N-terminal TBD-CRR module, wherein TBDs interact only with TPR, not with each other.
source: Furthermore, the absence of dimerization of an isolated TBD is consistent with its interactions within the N-terminal TBD-CRR module, wherein TBDs interact only with TPR, not with each other.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and SV AUC results.

claim: Isolated CRR showed no dimerization, suggesting that contacts between PH domains observed in the ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD dimer are not strong enough to allow the formation of a stable CRR dimer.
source: Isolated CRR showed no dimerization either, suggesting that contacts between PH domains observed in the ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD dimer are not strong enough to allow the formation of a stable CRR dimer and likely result from KD dimerization.
evidence: This is an inference based on SV AUC data and structural analysis.

claim: Contacts between PH domains likely result from KD dimerization.
source: Isolated CRR showed no dimerization either, suggesting that contacts between PH domains observed in the ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD dimer are not strong enough to allow the formation of a stable CRR dimer and likely result from KD dimerization.
evidence: This is an inference based on SV AUC data and structural analysis.

claim: SV AUC measurements with isolated domains and their pairs are consistent with the cryo-EM structure of C-terminally truncated ASK1.
source: Combined, our SV AUC measurements with isolated domains and their pairs are consistent with the cryo-EM structure of C-terminally truncated ASK1 and confirm that all three N-terminal domains are involved in homophilic interactions between ASK1 chains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined SV AUC and cryo-EM data.

claim: All three N-terminal domains are involved in homophilic interactions between ASK1 chains.
source: Combined, our SV AUC measurements with isolated domains and their pairs are consistent with the cryo-EM structure of C-terminally truncated ASK1 and confirm that all three N-terminal domains are involved in homophilic interactions between ASK1 chains.
evidence: This is supported by combined SV AUC and cryo-EM data.

claim: TRX1 binding has no effect on ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD dimerization.
source: Unexpectedly, SV AUC showed that TRX1 binding has no effect on ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by SV AUC data.

claim: TRX1 binding reduces the formation of higher oligomers of ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD.
source: However, when we compared c(s) distributions, we found a significant reduction in peak area, in the region of sedimentation coefficients 10–12 S, in the presence of TRX1. This result indicates that TRX1 prevents the formation of higher oligomers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by SV AUC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several TBD regions were significantly more protected from deuteration upon TRX1 binding.
source: The comparison of ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD deuteration profiles with and without TRX1 revealed that several TBD regions were significantly (more than twice the standard deviation and above 3%) less deuterated, that is, more protected, upon TRX1 binding (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4A and B and supplementary figures.

claim: Significant protection upon TRX1 binding was observed in TBD residues 128–143, 184–195, and 206–259.
source: More specifically, significant protection was observed in residues 128–143, 184–195, and especially in segments 206–259.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: Many of the protected TBD segments overlapped with regions previously identified by NMR as the TRX1 binding surface of TBD.
source: Many of these segments overlapped with regions previously identified by NMR as the TRX1 binding surface of TBD (Psenakova et al., 2020) and, moreover, included the flexible region between β5 and α5 containing C225 and C250 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previous NMR data and HDX-MS results.

claim: The protected TBD regions on the flexible outer surface near the interface between TBD and TPR may form a TRX1-binding site.
source: These regions on the flexible outer surface of the TBD near the interface between the TBD and the TPR of the opposite chain may form a TRX1-binding site.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data and structural analysis.

claim: TRX1 binding reduced deuteration in the α15 helix of the TPR domain.
source: This hypothesis is in line with the decrease in deuteration observed in the α15 helix of the TPR domain, which interfaces with TBD, in the adjacent α13, α14, and α19 helixes, and in the α13-α14, α14-α15, α17-α18, and α18-α19 loops (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Within the PH domain, the β-strand β9 and the β8-β9 loop were protected upon TRX1 binding.
source: Within the PH domain, the β-strand β9 and the β8-β9 loop, located near the α19 helix of the TPR, were also protected.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: TRX1 binding likely stabilizes the structure of TPR and PH regions and/or reduces their solvent accessibility.
source: Given the lower deuteration of these regions, TRX1 binding likely stabilizes their structure and/or reduces their solvent accessibility (e.g. through conformational change), as shown by changes in the deuteration of several KD regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data.

claim: TRX1 binding to TBD reduced deuteration near the active site and at the C-terminus of the KD.
source: TRX1 binding to TBD reduced deuteration near the active site and at the C-terminus of the KD (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The most protected area in KD upon TRX1 binding included residues 830–844, which form the activation segment.
source: The most protected area included residues 830–844, which form the activation segment and interact with the TPR domain.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: The region containing αEF, helix αG, and several loops also showed reduced deuteration upon TRX1 binding.
source: In addition to the activation segment, the region containing αEF (α24), the helix αG (α26) and the αD-αE (α22-α23), αF-αG (α25-α26), and αG-αH (α26-α26) loops also showed reduced deuteration.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: The protected KD regions likely interact with each other, forming a coherent area whose structure and/or access to solvent is affected by TRX1 binding.
source: Accordingly, these regions likely interact with each other, forming a coherent area whose structure and/or access to solvent is affected by TRX1 binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data.

claim: Significant protection was observed in residues 655–670, which form a linker connecting PH and KD.
source: Significant protection was also observed in residues 655–670, which form a linker connecting PH and KD (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The linker connecting PH and KD should be quite flexible as no interpretable density was found in this region.
source: This linker should be quite flexible as no interpretable density was found in this region, in either protomer.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: TRX1 binding reduced deuteration of the PH-KD linker, suggesting structural changes at the interface of PH and KD.
source: However, TRX1 binding reduced its deuteration, suggesting structural changes at the interface of PH and KD.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data.

claim: TRX1 binding to TBD significantly alters the interactions and structure of TBDs, leading to changes in interactions within CRRs and to conformational changes in KDs.
source: Taken together, our HDX-MS results indicate that TRX1 binding to TBD significantly alters the interactions and structure of TBDs, leading to changes in interactions within CRRs and to conformational changes in KDs, including in their activation segment and the C-terminus.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data.

claim: TRX1 interacts with ASK1 through its active site.
source: Based on comparisons of TRX1 deuteration profiles with and without ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD, the helix α2 regions and the β-strands β1, β3, and β4 (Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—figure supplements 6 and 7) are significantly protected.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4C and D and supplementary figures.

claim: The protected TRX1 regions include the highly conserved catalytic motif W31CGPC35.
source: This protection includes the highly conserved catalytic motif W31CGPC35, located at the N-terminus of the α2 helices, whose sulfhydryl groups are responsible for TRX-dependent redox activity (Holmgren et al., 1975).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data and citation to Holmgren et al., 1975.

claim: TRX1 binds to ASK1 through its active site, consistent with previous findings.
source: This result is in line with previous findings according to which TRX1 binds to ASK1 through its active site (Fujino et al., 2007; Kylarova et al., 2016; Psenakova et al., 2020; Saitoh et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data and multiple citations.

claim: Homophilic interactions between N-terminal domains are crucial for ASK1 activation.
source: Homophilic interactions between N-terminal domains are crucial for ASK1 activation, as shown by our structural analysis of the C-terminally truncated ASK1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis.

claim: ASK1 oligomerization is mediated by its C-terminal CC motif.
source: In addition to these interactions, ASK1 oligomerization is mediated by its C-terminal CC motif because the C-terminally truncated ASK1 has lower Thr838 phosphorylation levels and basal activity (Tobiume et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tobiume et al., 2002.

claim: The C-terminally truncated ASK1 has lower Thr838 phosphorylation levels and basal activity.
source: In addition to these interactions, ASK1 oligomerization is mediated by its C-terminal CC motif because the C-terminally truncated ASK1 has lower Thr838 phosphorylation levels and basal activity (Tobiume et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tobiume et al., 2002.

claim: The ASK1 construct with the first 384 residues can oligomerize.
source: Furthermore, the ASK1 construct with the first 384 residues of this protein, containing TBD and the N-terminal portion of TPR, can also oligomerize, as previously demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation (Fujino et al., 2007) and in line with our SV AUC measurements (Figure 3D) and with our cryo-EM analysis of the apo form of ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fujino et al., 2007 and SV AUC data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Interactions with the dimeric N-terminal TBD-CRR module may stabilize the active conformation of one of the two KDs.
source: Considering this position and the position of the activation segment, which is structured through interactions with the adjacent TPR and maintains a conformation competent for substrate binding, in the case of KDB (Figure 2B and C), interactions with the dimeric N-terminal TBD-CRR module may stabilize the active conformation of one of the two KDs.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: T838 is oriented toward the solvent, so its (auto)phosphorylation could further stabilize the activation segment.
source: Furthermore, located in the activation segment and known to play a key role in ASK1 activation (Tobiume et al., 2002), T838 is oriented toward the solvent, so its (auto)phosphorylation could further stabilize the activation segment through interactions with residues (e.g. K526) of the loop between α18 and α19 of TPR located nearby.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data and citation to Tobiume et al., 2002.

claim: ASK1 TBD is structurally heterogeneous and has a globular conformation resembling the thioredoxin fold.
source: In a recent study, we have shown that ASK1 TBD is structurally heterogeneous and has a globular conformation resembling the thioredoxin fold, with its C-terminal half (residues ~165–260) forming a TRX1-binding site (Psenakova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Psenakova et al., 2020.

claim: The C-terminal half of TBD (residues ~165–260) forms a TRX1-binding site.
source: In a recent study, we have shown that ASK1 TBD is structurally heterogeneous and has a globular conformation resembling the thioredoxin fold, with its C-terminal half (residues ~165–260) forming a TRX1-binding site (Psenakova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Psenakova et al., 2020.

claim: Residues ~165–260 of TBD form not only the solvent-accessible outer surface of the ASK1 dimer but also the binding interface with the TPR domain.
source: In this study, our cryo-EM structure revealed that these residues form not only the solvent-accessible outer surface of the ASK1 dimer but also the binding interface with the TPR domain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TRX1 binding significantly affects the structure of TBD and its interactions within the ASK1 dimer.
source: Consequently, TRX1 binding significantly affects the structure of TBD and its interactions within the ASK1 dimer.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data.

claim: The differences between the TPR of the present ASK1 structure and the crystal structure of CRR suggest that the ASK1 TPR domain is a flexible structure.
source: Considering the differences between the TPR of the present ASK1 structure and the crystal structure of CRR (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Weijman et al., 2017) and its position in the ASK1 dimer, the ASK1 TPR domain appears to be a flexible structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The structural flexibility of TPR enables communication between TBD and KD.
source: This structural flexibility enables communication between TBD and KD, as evidenced by structural changes in KD induced by TRX1 binding, and is in line with the role of TPR domains as structurally diverse scaffolding and binding modules, some of which are quite flexible, triggering allosteric effects, and supporting molecular switch functions (Perez-Riba and Itzhaki, 2019; Perez-Riba et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data and citations.

claim: TPR domains are structurally diverse scaffolding and binding modules, some of which are quite flexible, triggering allosteric effects, and supporting molecular switch functions.
source: This structural flexibility enables communication between TBD and KD, as evidenced by structural changes in KD induced by TRX1 binding, and is in line with the role of TPR domains as structurally diverse scaffolding and binding modules, some of which are quite flexible, triggering allosteric effects, and supporting molecular switch functions (Perez-Riba and Itzhaki, 2019; Perez-Riba et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Perez-Riba and Itzhaki, 2019 and Perez-Riba et al., 2018.

claim: Allosteric effects regulate the binding of Hif, a TPR protein, to histone complexes H2A-H2B and H3-H4.
source: For example, allosteric effects regulate the binding of Hif, a TPR protein, to histone complexes H2A-H2B and H3-H4 (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: The flexibility or conformational plasticity of CRR may be involved in substrate recruitment.
source: Moreover, the flexibility or conformational plasticity of CRR may be involved in substrate recruitment (Weijman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weijman et al., 2017.

claim: Many protein kinases are regulated through the phosphorylation of a residue(s) located in the activation segment.
source: Many protein kinases are regulated through the phosphorylation of a residue(s) located in the activation segment (Johnson et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johnson et al., 1996.

claim: Akt1 kinase is autoinhibited through intramolecular interactions between its PH and KD domains, limiting access to the activation segment.
source: For example, Akt1 kinase is autoinhibited through intramolecular interactions between its PH and KD domains, limiting access to the activation segment (Chu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chu et al., 2020.

claim: ASK1 is regulated by a mechanism involving structural changes in the activation segment.
source: Our HDX-MS data suggest that ASK1 is regulated by a similar mechanism involving structural changes in the activation segment.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data.

claim: TRX1 substantially reduces solvent access to the activation segment and/or decreases its flexibility.
source: As evidenced by the slower deuteration kinetics, TRX1 substantially reduces solvent access to this segment and/or decreases its flexibility by altering interactions either within KD and/or with TPR (Figure 4A and B), which may influence its phosphorylation on T838 within the signalosome.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: TRX1 likely contributes to ASK1 inhibition by reducing access to the activation segment.
source: In doing so, TRX1 likely contributes to ASK1 inhibition (Morita et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data and citations.

claim: Limiting access to residues of the activation segment regulated by phosphorylation may be a key regulatory event of ASK1 function.
source: Therefore, limiting access to residues of the activation segment regulated by phosphorylation may be thus a key regulatory event of ASK1 function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the HDX-MS data.

claim: In MAP3K BRAF, the helix αG is involved in binding to its substrate MEK1.
source: These regions are adjacent to the activation segment, and in MAP3K BRAF, the helix αG is involved in binding to its substrate MEK1 (Haling et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haling et al., 2014.

claim: TRX1 may function as an allosteric effector, changing the conformation of key regions of the KD domain.
source: Accordingly, TRX1 may function as an allosteric effector, changing the conformation of key regions of the KD domain when binding to TBDs and, therefore, inducing conformational changes transferred via CRRs.
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data.

claim: TRX1 binding alters homophilic interactions of the N-terminal domain rather than disrupting them.
source: Rather than disrupting homophilic interactions of the N-terminal domain, TRX1 binding alters them, since no significant deprotection was detected by HDX-MS.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: At intracellular ASK1 concentrations, TRX1 binding may reduce homophilic interactions of the N-terminal domains of ASK1.
source: However, at intracellular ASK1 concentrations, which are substantially lower than those used in our SV AUC and HDX-MS experiments, TRX1 binding may reduce homophilic interactions of the N-terminal domains of ASK1, as previously shown by immunoprecipitation analysis (Fujino et al., 2007).
evidence: This is speculation based on the difference between experimental and intracellular conditions, supported by citation to Fujino et al., 2007.

claim: Inactive ASK1 is bound to scaffolding 14-3-3 proteins, which recognize a motif containing phosphorylated S966.
source: Inactive ASK1 is bound to scaffolding 14-3-3 proteins, which recognize a motif containing phosphorylated S966, located at the C-terminus of KD (Goldman et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goldman et al., 2004 and Zhang et al., 1999.

claim: 14-3-3 proteins suppress the catalytic activity of ASK1 through an unknown mechanism.
source: 14-3-3 proteins suppress the catalytic activity of ASK1 through an unknown mechanism, albeit potentially involving suppression of homophilic interactions between N-terminal domains.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.

claim: ASK1 activation requires TRAF2/5/6 or Daxx recruitment.
source: In contrast, ASK1 activation requires TRAF2/5/6 or Daxx recruitment.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claim: TRAF2/5/6 and Daxx interact with CRR and enhance N-terminal homophilic interactions of ASK1 protomers.
source: These proteins interact with CRR and enhance N-terminal homophilic interactions of ASK1 protomers (Chang et al., 1998; Fujino et al., 2007; Gotoh and Cooper, 1998; Saitoh et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: TRAF2/5/6 or Daxx binding to CRR could stabilize the conformation of the ASK1 dimer, thereby promoting its activation.
source: Thus, TRAF2/5/6 or Daxx binding to CRR could stabilize the conformation of the ASK1 dimer, thereby promoting its activation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known interactions.

claim: C-terminal segments may affect interactions of N-terminal domains, including KDs.
source: Our structural analysis was performed with a C-terminally truncated ASK1 missing the CC motif and a C-terminal SAM domain, involved in ASK1 oligomerization. Thus, we cannot rule out the possibility that C-terminal segments may affect interactions of N-terminal domains, including KDs.
evidence: This is speculation about potential effects not observed in the current study.

claim: The structures of relevant complexes must be solved in subsequent studies to elucidate structural changes caused by TRX1 binding and other binding partners.
source: In addition, the structures of relevant complexes must be solved in subsequent studies to elucidate in detail structural changes caused by TRX1 binding, as well as other binding partners, and to fully understand how these interactions contribute to ASK1 regulation.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The findings open up opportunities for targeting interaction(s) responsible for ASK1 activation towards developing selective ASK1 signaling inhibitors.
source: Therefore, our findings open up opportunities for targeting (the) interaction(s) responsible for ASK1 activation towards developing selective ASK1 signaling inhibitors and ultimately pharmaceutical drugs for several inflammatory, cardiovascular, and neurodegenerative diseases, among others (Budas et al., 2018; Ogier et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications, supported by citations.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of ASK1 TBD-CRR-KD was determined at a nominal resolution of 3.7 Å.
source: Approximately 5780 micrograph movies enabled single-particle reconstructions of this protein at a nominal resolution of 3.7 Å, as further detailed in Methods and Supplementary file 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the methods and supplementary data.

claim: The final ASK1 model has been deposited in PDB/EMDB under accession code: 8QGY/EMD-18396.
source: The final model has been deposited in PDB/EMDB under accession code: 8QGY/EMD-18396.
evidence: This is a factual statement about data deposition.
